title: Job spoke right (Job 42:7–17)
hookLine: God says the friends were wrong and Job was right; Job prays for them
carry: the man who cried out was right

cards: Three friends sat with Job in the dust, then argued with him for a long stretch of the book. You must have done something, they said. God is just, so your suffering has a reason.
Confess, and it will get better. Job refused. He cursed the day he was born, demanded a hearing, called out to God.
Then God spoke from the whirlwind, and Job went quiet. A reader might expect the verdict to fall on Job. It falls somewhere else.

teach.b: God turns, not to Job, but to Eliphaz.

teach.h: YE HAVE NOT SPOKEN OF ME THE THING THAT IS RIGHT.
teach.b: In the King James words: "My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath."
The friends defended God and said all the careful, tidy things, and God says they were wrong. Job accused, protested, wept and asked why, and God calls him my servant and says he spoke right.
Readers still puzzle over what Job got right. Some say his honesty: he wouldn't pretend his suffering made sense. Others say he spoke to God, while his friends only spoke about God.
The text doesn't settle it, and this path won't either. Then a second turn.

teach.h: JOB PRAYS FOR THOSE WHO LECTURED HIM.
teach.b: The friends must bring an offering, and Job, the man they lectured, is to pray for them. And the LORD turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends.
His restoring begins there, in a prayer for the people who hurt him. His family and old acquaintances come to eat bread with him and comfort him. He is given twice as much as he had before.
He has daughters again, and the text names them, Jemima, Keziah and Keren-happuch, and says their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.
Some readers find this ending too neat; others hear a gift that never erases what was lost. Either way, the book ends with Job old and full of days.

how: Job belongs to the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh. Jews read and study it as a book that argues with God about suffering, and some readers take its last chapter as a model of praying for those who wronged you.

o: what God calls Eliphaz, who defended God
what Job calls the friends who sat with him
what God calls Job, who spoke right

s: in the last chapter, God says the friends spoke right and Job spoke wrong
it's the other way round: God says the friends were wrong, and that Job spoke the thing that is right.
Job's restoring begins when he prays for his friends
the text says the LORD turned his captivity when he prayed for his friends.
the last chapter names Job's daughters
Jemima, Keziah and Keren-happuch, and their father gives them an inheritance.

games.q: you're Job. the friends who lectured you have been told they were wrong. what do you do?
o: tell them you were right all along.
games.why: Job prays for them, and the text says his own restoring begins right there.

practice: This week in Job ran from a cursed day, through friends explaining pain, a man asking to speak to the Almighty, a redeemer who lives and wisdom that can't be bought, to a whirlwind.

Now bring to mind someone ordinary who hurt you, maybe with words meant to help, and say their name once, inside. If you pray, pray for them in your own words or your tradition's; if not, simply wish them one good thing.

wordCard.voice: My servant. God calls Job, not the friends with neat answers, my servant, and says he spoke right. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the man who cried out was right. His restoring began with a prayer for his friends. Day eight hundred forty-seven, done.
